objective.text: Choose a daylight-saving transition fixture that distinguishes a calendar-day increment from 24 elapsed hours.

difficulty.rationale: Select an observation that separates local civil-time requirements from fixed-duration arithmetic.

runtime.sapi: CLI unless the stated context specifies otherwise
runtime.errorPolicy: E_ALL; no custom handler unless explicitly shown. 64-bit PHP; UTC; C locale.

assumptions: Run in a fresh PHP process using only the displayed files and inputs.

The requirement is the same local clock time on the next calendar date in Europe/Zurich. In 2026, clocks advance from 02:00 to 03:00 on March 29. Inputs are noon, so no requested local time is ambiguous or nonexistent.

files.source:
<?php

function tomorrowAtSameTime(string $start): string
{
    $date = new DateTimeImmutable($start, new DateTimeZone('Europe/Zurich'));

    return $date->add(new DateInterval('PT24H'))->format('Y-m-d H:i');
}

options.rationale: The next local noon is only 23 elapsed hours away; adding 24 hours instead reaches 13:00.
The offset is unchanged across this interval, so the defect is not exercised.

explanation.trace: The implementation returns March 29 at 13:00 for the spring fixture. Replacing PT24H with P1D preserves noon on all four dates.

objective.text: Test literal substring semantics separately from safe SQL parameter binding.

difficulty.rationale: Recognize that a bound LIKE value still contains pattern operators unless the application escapes them.

runtime.sapi: CLI unless the stated context specifies otherwise
runtime.errorPolicy: E_ALL; no custom handler unless explicitly shown. 64-bit PHP; UTC; C locale.

assumptions: Run in a fresh PHP process using only the displayed files and inputs.

The SQLite fixture contains exactly abc, a_c and zzz. Search must treat every input character literally, including % and _. Results are sorted by name. The exclamation mark is the declared LIKE escape character.

files.source:
<?php

$pdo = new PDO('sqlite::memory:');
$pdo->exec('CREATE TABLE names (name TEXT NOT NULL)');
$pdo->exec("INSERT INTO names VALUES ('abc'), ('a_c'), ('zzz')");

function searchNames(PDO $pdo, string $needle): array
{
    $escaped = $needle;
    $statement = $pdo->prepare("SELECT name FROM names WHERE name LIKE :pattern ESCAPE '!' ORDER BY name");
    $statement->execute(['pattern' => '%' . $escaped . '%']);

    return $statement->fetchAll(PDO::FETCH_COLUMN);
}

records.stem: Which needle and expected result exposes the search defect?

options.rationale: The plain letters need no pattern escaping, so both implementations agree.
options.misconception: Assuming an ordinary successful search covers literal metacharacters.

options.rationale: An unescaped underscore matches any single character, so the defective query returns all three nonempty names.
This needle has no wildcard and does not expose the defect.
options.misconception: Testing a second ordinary term instead of the pattern boundary.

options.rationale: Both implementations correctly find no q; the false-positive behavior needs a wildcard-bearing input.
options.misconception: Assuming a no-result test proves every literal query remains literal.

explanation.summary: Binding keeps the value out of SQL syntax, but LIKE interprets % and _ inside that value as pattern operators. A literal-search adapter must escape the escape character and both wildcard characters.
explanation.trace: The defective pattern %_% matches every nonempty fixture name. Escaping the underscore creates %!_%, which matches only a_c.
